processing: No fixed standard is documented for this name. It would follow the usual Yunnan gongfu black tea steps of withering, rolling, full oxidation and drying, using tippy material.
harvest_season: Not documented for this name. Bud-heavy Dian Hong is generally picked in early spring.
appearance_dry: As the name suggests, fine strands with plenty of golden tip.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear orange-red, as with other tippy Dian Hong.
appearance_wet: Typically soft coppery buds and young leaf, as with other tippy Dian Hong.
taste_profile: Little is recorded for this name itself. Tippy Yunnan black teas in general run sweet and smooth with light malt and very little astringency.

brewing.notes: General advice for tippy Dian Hong: buds extract quickly, so keep the water a little off the boil and the early steeps short.

vintage_note: No selling convention is recorded for this name. Like other Dian Hong it is usually sold by the current year's harvest, with early spring tippy lots costing more, and is best drunk within a couple of years.
description:
Jin Si, golden silk, is a trade name for a tippy Yunnan black tea: Dian Hong with fine, golden, thread-like strands. It describes how the leaf looks and does not mark out a defined place or standard.

Little is documented about how this particular name is made. What can be said is what is typical of its class: large-leaf Yunnan material goes through withering, rolling, full oxidation and drying, and the gold comes from the proportion of downy buds.

Expect the broad Dian Hong character rather than something unique: sweet, smooth, lightly malty, with little astringency. Short steeps and slightly cooler water suit the buds.

When buying, treat the name as a description of appearance. Ask the seller for the county, the harvest date and how much of the leaf is really bud, since two teas called golden silk may have little in common.
history: Little is documented about this name. It belongs to the wider Dian Hong story, which starts with Feng Shaoqiu's trial black tea made in Shunning, now Fengqing, in 1938. When Jin Si came into use as a trade name, and who first used it, is not recorded.
